items.prompt: What happens at the very start, when a sperm and an egg combine?

options.label: The two cells stay separate side by side
options.feedback: They do not stay apart. The whole point of the meeting is that they merge into one.

options.label: The sperm dissolves and disappears
options.feedback: The sperm's outer parts are shed, but its genetic material is not lost — it enters the egg and stays.

options.label: Their genetic material joins to form one new cell
options.feedback: Correct.

options.label: The egg splits into two smaller eggs
options.feedback: Fertilization joins two cells into one; it does not split one cell into two.

items.ok_line: Two sets of instructions become one.
items.ko_line: Think about what a sperm and an egg each carry, and what happens the instant they meet.
items.exp_text: A sperm carries one set of chromosomes and an egg carries another, and when they meet, the sperm's nucleus enters the egg and the two sets merge inside one membrane. That merged set becomes the working instructions for a new body, copied afterward into every cell that grows from that meeting.

items.prompt: How does one fertilized cell turn into a baby made of countless cells?

options.label: It repeatedly splits into two, then two become four, and so on
options.feedback: Correct.

options.label: It grows bigger without splitting
options.feedback: A single oversized cell could never form fingers or organs. It has to divide, not just swell.

options.label: Other cells join it from outside
options.feedback: Nothing arrives from outside to add to the count. Every cell in the body traces back to that same starting cell.

options.label: It turns into a different kind of cell each day
options.feedback: Changing type is a later step for some cells, but it does not explain how the cell count grows at all.

items.ok_line: Splitting, not growing, is how the numbers rise.
items.ko_line: No cells arrive from outside — the increase has to come from within the cell itself.
items.exp_text: The fertilized cell splits into two identical cells, and each of those splits again, so the count doubles again and again with each round. Repeating that simple split, over and over, is how a whole body gets built up — no new material brought in, just division.

items.prompt: What has to happen for a very early embryo to keep developing inside the mother?

options.label: It floats freely in the uterus the whole time
options.feedback: Floating free lasts only the first few days. After that it needs to attach, or it cannot draw on the mother's supply.

options.label: It attaches to the outside of the uterus
options.feedback: Attaching to the outside would leave it with no access to the mother's blood supply inside the lining.

options.label: It travels to the mother's bloodstream directly
options.feedback: It never enters the mother's bloodstream directly. It stays inside the uterus and connects through the lining instead.

options.label: It burrows into the lining of the uterus
options.feedback: Correct.

items.ok_line: It has to attach before it can draw on the mother's supply.
items.ko_line: Being free-floating is only the very first stage. Ask what comes right after that.
items.exp_text: After several days of traveling and dividing, the ball of cells reaches the uterus and burrows into its thickened lining, a step called implantation. Once anchored there, it can begin drawing on the mother's blood supply for everything it needs to keep growing.

items.prompt: How does a growing baby get oxygen and nutrients before it can breathe or eat?

options.label: By swallowing amniotic fluid for food
options.feedback: Swallowing fluid happens later and mostly practices the muscles used for swallowing — it is not the baby's food source.

options.label: Through the placenta, from the mother's blood
options.feedback: Correct.

options.label: Through the skin, absorbing them directly from the fluid
options.feedback: Skin does not absorb nutrients from the surrounding fluid. The exchange happens through a dedicated organ instead.

options.label: The baby doesn't need them until birth
options.feedback: A growing body needs a constant supply well before birth, not a sudden delivery at the end.

items.ok_line: Everything the baby needs arrives through that one organ.
items.ko_line: The baby isn't yet breathing or eating in the usual sense, so where would supplies come from instead?
items.exp_text: The placenta is an organ built from tissue of both mother and baby, and inside it the mother's blood vessels and the baby's blood vessels run close together without ever mixing. Oxygen and nutrients cross that thin barrier into the baby's blood, while carbon dioxide and waste cross back the other way.

items.prompt: What is the umbilical cord for?

options.label: It holds the baby in place inside the uterus
options.feedback: Position is kept by the fluid and the walls of the uterus around it, not by the cord.

options.label: It lets the baby breathe air before birth
options.feedback: There is no air inside the uterus to breathe. The cord carries blood, not air.

options.label: It carries blood between the placenta and the baby
options.feedback: Correct.

options.label: It connects the baby's stomach to the mother's stomach
options.feedback: The two digestive systems are never linked. What links mother and baby is a blood supply, not a shared gut.

items.ok_line: A two-way line running to and from the placenta.
items.ko_line: The cord is a passage for blood, not for air or food directly.
items.exp_text: The umbilical cord is a flexible tube of blood vessels running from the baby's navel to the placenta, carrying blood back and forth between the two. Blood loaded with oxygen and nutrients flows in through the cord, and blood carrying waste flows back out through it.

items.prompt: What is the fluid-filled sac around a developing baby for?

options.label: It cushions the baby and lets it move freely
options.feedback: Correct.

options.label: It filters the baby's blood
options.feedback: Filtering waste out of the blood is not something this fluid does. Its role is around the baby, not inside its blood supply.

options.label: It keeps the baby warm by trapping air
options.feedback: There is no trapped air here — the sac is filled with fluid, and warmth comes mainly from the mother's body.

options.label: It supplies the baby's oxygen directly
options.feedback: Oxygen reaches the baby through the placenta, not through the fluid it floats in.

items.ok_line: Fluid, not air, does the cushioning.
items.ko_line: This sac protects and gives room to move — other structures handle feeding and breathing.
items.exp_text: The amniotic sac holds fluid that surrounds the baby completely, spreading out any bump or squeeze from outside so it never reaches the baby directly. Floating in that fluid, the baby can also kick, turn and stretch its growing limbs without pressing against anything solid.

items.prompt: Which organ starts working while the rest of the baby is still forming?

options.label: The lungs
options.feedback: The lungs stay filled with fluid and cannot work until birth brings the first breath of air.

options.label: The stomach
options.feedback: Digestion is not needed yet, since food arrives through the placenta rather than the mouth and stomach.

options.label: The kidneys
options.feedback: The kidneys do form early, but they are not the organ that starts pulsing and moving blood before anything else takes shape.

options.label: The heart
options.feedback: Correct.

items.ok_line: It starts pulsing long before it looks like a heart.
items.ko_line: This organ isn't ready for its usual job yet — but one organ nearby is already beating.
items.exp_title: Beating before it looks like anything
items.exp_text: The heart is among the first organs to take shape, forming from a simple tube that folds and begins to pulse while the rest of the embryo is still a small cluster of developing tissue. That beating tube goes on folding into the chambers of a full heart, pumping blood through the embryo's own tiny vessels before arms or legs have appeared.

items.prompt: How do arms and legs begin to form on a developing embryo?

options.label: They appear all at once, fully formed
options.feedback: Nothing about a limb arrives complete. Every part of it is built up gradually from something much smaller.

options.label: As small buds that grow and gradually shape into limbs
options.feedback: Correct.

options.label: By splitting off from the torso as separate pieces
options.feedback: A limb is never a separate piece that splits away — it grows outward while staying joined to the body the whole time.

options.label: As full-sized limbs that later shrink to fit
options.feedback: A limb never starts oversized and shrinks. It starts tiny and grows larger as the embryo does.

items.ok_line: Small buds first, shaped gradually from there.
items.ko_line: Nothing about a limb arrives complete or all at once — it is built up in stages.
items.exp_text: Arms and legs start as small bulges on the sides of the embryo, called limb buds, where cells multiply fast and push outward. Inside each bud, some cells become bone and muscle while the tissue between future fingers dies away, freeing separate fingers from what was a solid paddle shape.

items.prompt: When do a person's fingerprints form, and can they ever change?

options.label: They form at birth and change during childhood
options.feedback: They are already set well before birth, not formed at the moment of birth itself.

options.label: They form gradually throughout life
options.feedback: The pattern is not still being drawn as a person ages. It is fixed long before that.

options.label: They form before birth and stay the same for life
options.feedback: Correct.

options.label: They form before birth but change with age
options.feedback: The timing is right, but the pattern itself does not change afterward, even as the finger grows larger.

items.ok_line: Set before birth, unchanged for a lifetime after.
items.ko_line: Think about why the very same pattern always grows back after a scrape or cut.
items.exp_text: The ridged pattern on a fingertip forms before birth, as the skin there grows faster than the layer beneath it and buckles into ridges and swirls. Once that buckled shape is set, new skin keeps following the same underlying pattern after every scrape, growing back the same ridges rather than a fresh design.

items.prompt: Why does a baby usually end up positioned head-down before birth?

options.label: Gravity and the shape of the uterus favor that position
options.feedback: Correct.

options.label: The baby chooses that position on purpose
options.feedback: Nothing about this is a deliberate choice. It follows from shape and weight, not intention.

options.label: The head is lighter than the rest of the body
options.feedback: The head is actually the heavier, rounder end of the baby, which is exactly why it settles downward.

options.label: The umbilical cord pulls it into place
options.feedback: The cord is flexible and does not pull the baby into any particular position.

items.ok_line: Shape and weight settle the baby into place, not choice.
items.ko_line: Nothing about the baby decides this on its own — look instead at the space it is fitting into.
items.exp_text: As a baby grows late in pregnancy, the uterus narrows toward the bottom and widens near the top, so the baby's rounder, heavier head settles into the narrower lower space while its more flexible legs curl into the roomier space above. That position also lines the head up with the opening it will need to pass through during birth.
